2. STEP 1 — INDEPENDENT DESIGN CLASSIFICATION & TOOL SELECTION (`RISK_OF_BIAS.md` §1):
   Classify the study's actual design from its Methods section, then select the matching appraisal tool:
   - `"RoB 2 (parallel-trial variant)"`: Individually randomized controlled trial. Rate all 5 domains (`D1` Randomization process; `D2` Deviations from intended interventions; `D3` Missing outcome data; `D4` Measurement of the outcome; `D5` Selection of the reported result) as `"Low"`, `"Some concerns"`, or `"High"`, and overall rating as `"Low"`, `"Some concerns"`, or `"High"`.
   - `"RoB 2 (cluster-randomized trials variant)"`: Cluster-randomized trial (villages, compounds, neighbourhoods, schools, utilities randomized as clusters). Rate all 6 domains (`D1a` Randomization process; `D1b` Timing of identification or recruitment of participants within clusters; `D2` Deviations from intended interventions; `D3` Missing outcome data; `D4` Measurement of the outcome; `D5` Selection of the reported result) as `"Low"`, `"Some concerns"`, or `"High"`, and overall rating as `"Low"`, `"Some concerns"`, or `"High"`.
   - `"ROBINS-I"`: Non-randomized study of an intervention / policy with a genuine comparator (DiD, IV, RDD, PSM, ITS, controlled before-after, comparative longitudinal/panel evaluation). Rate all 7 domains (`D1` Bias due to confounding; `D2` Bias in selection of participants into the study; `D3` Bias in classification of interventions; `D4` Bias due to deviations from intended interventions; `D5` Bias due to missing data; `D6` Bias in measurement of outcomes; `D7` Bias in selection of the reported result — note `No information` honestly if no pre-analysis plan/protocol exists) as `"Low"`, `"Moderate"`, `"Serious"`, `"Critical"`, or `"No information"`, and overall rating in the same vocabulary. Do NOT assign single-case histories with no comparator arm to ROBINS-I!
   - `"JBI Critical Appraisal Checklist for Analytical Cross Sectional Studies"`: Quantitative cross-sectional survey / observational regression without a quasi-experimental intervention structure. Rate all 8 items (`Q1` Inclusion criteria in sample clearly defined; `Q2` Study subjects and setting described in detail; `Q3` Exposure measured validly and reliably; `Q4` Objective, standard criteria used for measurement of condition; `Q5` Confounding factors identified; `Q6` Strategies to deal with confounding factors stated; `Q7` Outcomes measured validly and reliably; `Q8` Appropriate statistical analysis used) as `"Yes"`, `"No"`, `"Unclear"`, or `"Not applicable"`. Provide overall narrative judgment (`"Low concern"`, `"Some concern"`, or `"High concern"` — no numeric score).
   - `"JBI Critical Appraisal Checklist for Cohort Studies"`: Observational comparative cohort design (not framed as a ROBINS-I intervention). Rate all 11 items (`Q1` Similar groups from same population; `Q2` Exposures measured similarly; `Q3` Exposure measured validly/reliably; `Q4` Confounding factors identified; `Q5` Strategies to deal with confounding stated; `Q6` Participants free of outcome at start; `Q7` Outcomes measured validly/reliably; `Q8` Follow-up time reported and sufficient; `Q9` Follow-up complete or loss explored; `Q10` Strategies to address incomplete follow-up utilized; `Q11` Appropriate statistical analysis used) as `"Yes"`, `"No"`, `"Unclear"`, or `"Not applicable"`, plus narrative overall judgment (`"Low concern"`, `"Some concern"`, `"High concern"`).
   - `"CASP Qualitative Checklist"`: Primary qualitative study (interviews, ethnography, focus groups, qualitative documentary/field case study). Rate all 10 items (`Q1` Clear statement of aims; `Q2` Qualitative methodology appropriate; `Q3` Research design appropriate to address aims; `Q4` Recruitment strategy appropriate to aims; `Q5` Data collected in a way that addressed research issue; `Q6` Relationship between researcher and participants adequately considered [reflexivity]; `Q7` Ethical issues considered; `Q8` Data analysis sufficiently rigorous; `Q9` Clear statement of findings; `Q10` How valuable is the research [narrative assessment]). Rate Q1-Q9 `"Yes"`, `"No"`, or `"Can't tell"`, and Q10 narratively; give narrative `overall_rating` (e.g. `"Low methodological concern"`, `"Moderate concern (X Can't tell / No items)"`, `"High methodological concern"` — no numeric score).
   - `"MMAT (Mixed Methods Appraisal Tool)"`: Genuine mixed-methods primary study combining qualitative AND quantitative empirical components (do NOT assign purely quantitative or purely qualitative studies to MMAT). Rate Screening `S1`-`S2`, Qualitative `1.1`-`1.5`, the matching Quantitative 5-item block (`2.1`-`2.5` randomized, `3.1`-`3.5` non-randomized, or `4.1`-`4.5` descriptive), AND Mixed-Methods integration `5.1`-`5.5` (`5.1` adequate rationale for mixed methods; `5.2` components effectively integrated; `5.3` outputs of integration adequately interpreted; `5.4` divergences/inconsistencies adequately addressed; `5.5` components adhere to quality criteria of each tradition) as `"Yes"`, `"No"`, or `"Can't tell"`. Per MMAT 2018 rules, NEVER compute a numeric score; provide a concise criterion-grounded narrative `overall_rating` noting that overall quality cannot exceed the weakest component.
   - `"AMSTAR 2"`: Secondary systematic review, meta-analysis, or scoping review with an explicit systematic search/screening method (NEVER apply AMSTAR 2 to non-systematic narrative literature reviews!). Rate all 16 items `Q1`-`Q16` (explicitly marking critical domains `Q2`, `Q4`, `Q7`, `Q9`, `Q11`, `Q13`, `Q15`) as `"Yes"`, `"Partial Yes"` (where applicable), `"No"`, or `"Not applicable (no meta-analysis)"`, and apply AMSTAR 2 overall confidence (`"High"`, `"Moderate"`, `"Low"`, `"Critically Low"`).
   - `"Legal Institutional Evidence Appraisal Framework"`: Doctrinal-empirical hybrid, jurimetric analysis, or institutional/legal-historical case study that fits NONE of the six conventional designs above. Rate all 13 narrative domains (`D1` Legal source accuracy; `D2` Jurisdictional specificity; `D3` Exposure definition; `D4` Outcome definition; `D5` Sampling transparency; `D6` Selection process; `D7` Measurement transparency; `D8` Causal identification; `D9` Treatment of confounding; `D10` Institutional context; `D11` Replication potential; `D12` Coding transparency; `D13` Researcher reflexivity) as `"strong"`, `"adequate"`, `"weak"`, or `"not assessable"`. Explicitly frame `overall_rating` as a structured non-validated judgment (NEVER a numeric composite score!).
   - `"NONE"`: Use when the study fits NONE of the listed instruments (e.g., pure mathematical/simulation optimization model with no empirical sample, or non-systematic narrative essay/review with no primary empirical method and no systematic search). Set `overall_rating = "NOT APPLICABLE (design fits no listed tool)"`, explain clearly in `why_tool_chosen` and `overall_narrative_summary` rather than forcing an inappropriate checklist, and still fill the 7 `cross_tool_domains` honestly from the paper!

cross_tool_domains.attrition: Low concern for primary public-good outcomes (all 570 Oaxaca municipalities have complete INEGI census/conteo data, with 6 non-usos municipalities excluded solely for common-support trimming, leaving n = 564); Moderate concern / insufficient information for auxiliary survey analyses (Table 1 item sample sizes drop from 568 to 362 without explanation of total sample size or non-response, and Table 5 reports unexplained sample counts of Treated = 412 and Control = 228, summing to 640 > 570 municipalities).
cross_tool_domains.confounding: Serious risk: Although first-differences remove time-invariant municipal unobservables, the propensity score model conditions on multiple post-1995 variables measured after the 1995 constitutional reform (2000 census per-capita GDP residuals, 2000 locality territorial concentration, 1990-2010 average indigenous-language share, 1990-2000 religious/ethnic fractionalization, and contemporaneous spatial lag of neighboring usos status). Baseline public-good coverage levels and pre-1995 trends (e.g., 1980-1990) are excluded from the propensity score, common support is extremely thin in the top block (212 treated vs. 4 control municipalities in Block 7), and poverty-formula federal infrastructure transfers (FAIS/FISM introduced in 1997) create plausible time-varying confounding and catch-up/ceiling dynamics.
cross_tool_domains.legal_measurement_quality: Moderate quality: Formal municipal governance status (usos y costumbres vs. political party elections under Oaxaca's 1995 constitutional reform) is grounded in official state electoral law and institutional rules (including fiscal transfer rules under FAIS/FISM). However, heterogeneous customary practices are collapsed into a static binary indicator fixed at the post-2000 count (418 usos municipalities), ignoring pre-1995 de facto customary governance and 1995-2000 regime switchers even when evaluating 1990-2000 changes.
cross_tool_domains.measurement_bias: Low risk for primary infrastructure outcomes (standardized, uniform INEGI national census and intercensal population count household enumerations across both usos and party municipalities), though Moderate concern applies to unvalidated subjective perception items in the auxiliary 2009 survey (Table 1).
cross_tool_domains.outcome_measurement_quality: Moderate quality: Household water and sewerage access are derived from objective, standardized national census/conteo enumerations (INEGI 1990, 1995, 2000, 2005, 2010), ensuring consistent administrative coverage measurement across municipalities, but the paper reports only coarse municipal household coverage percentages without specifying exact census definitions (e.g., piped connection vs. public tap, network sewerage vs. septic tank) or water/sanitation service quality, continuity, or potability, and percentage rate-of-change (%Delta) metrics are highly sensitive to near-zero baseline denominators.
cross_tool_domains.reporting_bias: Moderate risk (no pre-analysis plan/protocol): No pre-registration or study protocol exists. Only one propensity-score specification and kernel matching estimator are presented without robustness checks using strictly pre-treatment covariates or alternative matching/panel estimators; narrative conclusions overstate mixed results across four overlapping time windows and two functional forms (e.g., claiming faster education/literacy gains based on one p < 0.10 estimate out of eight cells, and emphasizing sub-period sewerage %Delta gains despite null 1990-2010 effects); and Tables 2-5 contain typesetting omissions of minus signs and inconsistent sample counts.
cross_tool_domains.selection_bias: Moderate risk: The primary analysis covers nearly the entire municipal universe of Oaxaca (564 of 570 municipalities within common support; 418 treated, 146 controls), minimizing sample exclusion bias, but treatment assignment is self-selected by communities in 1995, treatment status is fixed retroactively at the year-2000 roster (418 usos municipalities after post-1995 switching), common-support trimming relies on post-treatment covariates, and Table 5 reports an unexplained sample size discrepancy (412 treated + 228 control = 640 municipalities).

domain_ratings.justification: Serious risk of bias. While first-differences eliminate time-invariant municipal unobservables, the propensity score model used to match usos and party municipalities conditions on post-intervention covariates measured after the September/November 1995 Oaxaca constitutional reform—including 2000 census per-capita GDP residuals, 2000 locality territorial concentration, 1990–2010 average indigenous language share, 1990–2000 average fractionalization indices, and the contemporaneous spatial lag of neighboring usos municipalities—introducing post-treatment conditioning bias. Furthermore, the propensity score omits pre-1995 public good levels and pre-trends (no 1980–1990 parallel-trends test is reported), common support overlap is severely imbalanced in the highest propensity stratum (Block 7 matches 212 treated municipalities against only 4 control municipalities, and Block 4 shows a road-distance difference of 4.55 with SE 1.99), and post-1997 poverty-formula federal infrastructure transfers (FAIS/FISM) alongside lower initial service levels create unaddressed time-varying confounding and catch-up effects.

domain_ratings.domain_name: Bias in selection of participants into the study
domain_ratings.justification: Moderate risk of bias. Strengths include starting from the complete census universe of all 570 municipalities in Oaxaca and retaining 564 within common support (418 treated, 146 controls) for the primary public-goods evaluation. However, selection into the analytic common-support sample depends on a propensity score estimated from post-1995 census variables, treatment group membership is defined using the stabilized post-2000 roster of 418 usos municipalities even for intervals starting in 1990 and 1995, and the secondary governance analysis in Table 5 reports an unexplained sample count (Treated = 412, Control = 228; total = 640) that exceeds the 570 municipalities in Oaxaca.

Moderate risk of bias. De jure governance regime (usos y costumbres vs. political party system) is an official state electoral classification following Oaxaca's 1995 constitutional reform. However, the authors note that many municipalities already practiced customary governance informally de facto before 1995, that 412 municipalities adopted usos in November 1995 while 6 joined later (reaching 418 by 2000; Fig. 2 also notes fewer than 10 kept party elections temporarily), and that the analysis applies the static post-2000 binary classification across all windows—including 1990–2000, half of which predates the 1995 reform.

domain_ratings.domain_name: Bias due to deviations from intended interventions
domain_ratings.justification: Moderate risk of bias. Although usos formally prohibits political party participation in municipal elections, the authors note that in practice political parties are sometimes associated with candidates. More importantly, major post-1997 federal co-interventions—specifically formula-based municipal social infrastructure transfers (FAIS/FISM) governed by poverty indicators and conditional cash transfers (Progresa/Oportunidades, Note 8)—expanded concurrently and could differentially affect impoverished indigenous usos municipalities relative to controls where poverty-formula inputs were imperfectly balanced.

Moderate risk of bias overall (Low for primary census public-goods outcomes; Moderate/unclear for auxiliary survey outcomes). For the primary water, sewerage, electricity, and illiteracy outcomes (Table 4), INEGI census and population count data are complete for all 570 municipalities in Oaxaca, with only 6 control municipalities dropped for common-support trimming (n = 564). However, in Table 1 (2009 Oaxaca survey) valid responses vary substantially across items (from n = 568 down to n = 362) with no reporting of overall sample size or non-response, and Table 5 (2002 municipal president survey and SNIM administrative data) provides no missing-data accounting while reporting inconsistent group totals.

Low risk of bias for primary public-good outcomes. Municipal household coverage of water, sewerage, electricity, and illiteracy is measured from standardized, nationwide INEGI decennial censuses (1990, 2000, 2010) and intercensal population counts (1995, 2005) collected independently of the study and identically across usos and party municipalities, making differential measurement error between governance regimes unlikely (though coverage percentages are coarse and do not capture water potability or continuity, and Table 1's descriptive governance perceptions rely on unvalidated self-reports).

domain_ratings.domain_name: Bias in selection of the reported result
domain_ratings.justification: Moderate risk of bias (no pre-analysis plan or registered protocol exists). Beyond the absence of a pre-specified protocol, the authors present only a single propensity-score probit specification and kernel-matching estimator without testing sensitivity to strictly pre-1995 covariates or alternative matching/regression estimators. Across four overlapping census intervals (1990–2000, 2000–2010, 1995–2005, 1990–2010) and two outcome transformations (level change Delta vs. percentage rate of change %Delta), narrative conclusions selectively highlight favorable cells—claiming usos improves education/literacy and sewerage faster even though illiteracy is marginally significant (p < 0.10) in only 1 of 8 cells and sewerage ATTs over the full 1990–2010 period are statistically null—and Tables 2–5 exhibit systematic typesetting omissions of negative signs.

raw_response.overall_narrative_summary: Diaz-Cayeros, Magaloni, and Ruiz-Euler (2014) conduct a comparative observational policy evaluation of Oaxaca's 1995 constitutional reform recognizing indigenous customary municipal governance (usos y costumbres) versus political party governance across 570 municipalities (564 on common support), combining kernel propensity score matching with first-differences across 1990–2010 census/conteo waves. Under ROBINS-I, the overall risk of bias is Serious, driven primarily by Domain 1 (Confounding): although first-differences remove time-invariant municipal unobservables, the propensity score conditions on multiple post-1995 covariates measured after the 1995 reform (including 2000 census GDP residuals, 2000 locality concentration, 1990–2010 indigenous-language share, and contemporaneous spatial lag of neighboring usos status), omits pre-reform public-good levels and pre-1995 trend checks, suffers from severe support thinness in the highest propensity block (212 treated municipalities matched against just 4 controls in Block 7), and faces plausible time-varying confounding from post-1997 poverty-formula federal infrastructure transfers (FAIS/FISM) and baseline catch-up effects. Moderate concerns also arise in selection/sample reporting (retroactive use of the 2000 usos roster and an unexplained 412 treated / 228 control count in Table 5), intervention classification (pre-1995 de facto customary governance and 1995–2000 switchers, plus inclusion of pre-reform years in 1990–2000 differences), missing-data reporting in auxiliary surveys, and selective narrative emphasis across multiple overlapping periods and level vs. percentage-change metrics in the absence of a pre-analysis plan (notably, water coverage ATTs are uniformly null across all periods, and 1990–2010 sewerage ATTs are also statistically insignificant despite positive 1995–2005 and 2000–2010 rate-of-change estimates). Primary infrastructure outcome measurement from standardized INEGI censuses carries Low risk of differential measurement bias.
raw_response.study_design_identified: Quasi-experimental comparative policy evaluation using kernel propensity score matching (PSM) combined with first-differences panel estimation across municipal census waves (with auxiliary cross-sectional survey comparisons)
raw_response.where_found_summary: Research design and identification overview in Summary and Section 1 ([PDF Pages 1–2]) and Section 2 ([PDF Pages 3–4]); institutional comparison and auxiliary 2009 survey cross-tabulation in Section 3 ([PDF Pages 4–7], Table 1); propensity score matching methodology and covariate definitions in Section 4 ([PDF Pages 7–8]); balance tests, matched first-differences ATT estimates for water/sewerage/electricity/illiteracy, and electoral/civic estimates in Section 5 ([PDF Pages 8–11], Tables 2–5, Fig. 2); methodological footnotes in Notes ([PDF Pages 12–13]).
raw_response.why_tool_chosen: ROBINS-I is the exact matching instrument under RISK_OF_BIAS.md §1 because the study is a non-randomized comparative evaluation of a formal legal/institutional governance intervention (municipal adoption of usos y costumbres following Oaxaca's 1995 constitutional reform versus a political-party governance comparator arm) estimated via propensity score matching (PSM) and first-differences across census waves. MMAT was not selected because the paper's explicit 'multi-method approach' ([PDF Page 4]) refers to combining PSM with first-differences rather than a qualitative-quantitative mixed-methods design; brief background references to field observations in Section 3 lack any qualitative sampling, data collection, or analysis protocol.
